title: Northpeak AI x Redwood — Dedicated technical deep dive (throughput + shapes)
next_steps: Redwood to send a proposed benchmark plan (workload assumptions + prompt length distribution template) and a short list of candidate Dedicated shapes (L4/A100/H100) by EOD Feb 14.
Northpeak to provide 20–30 representative prompts (or a prompt-length histogram + output length targets) and peak concurrency goals by Feb 18.
Redwood to run baselines on 2 shapes (A100 80GB and H100) and share results + recommended tier by Feb 21.
Jordan to draft a Dedicated proposal (capacity + tier + burst policy + pricing range) for review in the week of Feb 24.
Schedule a follow-up review call after benchmark results are ready (target Feb 24 or Feb 25).
body:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: Northpeak AI x Redwood — Dedicated technical deep dive (throughput + shapes)
Date: Feb 13, 2025
Time: 11:06am–12:02pm PT
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Jordan Blake (AE), Sofia Ivanova (Runtime scheduling), Omar El-Sayed (Runtime throughput)
Northpeak AI: Maya Chen (Head of ML Platform), Arjun Rao (Staff Engineer, Inference), Priya Nair (SRE/Infra), Eli Kaplan (Product)

Auto Summary (generated)
- Northpeak is evaluating Redwood Dedicated primarily for predictable throughput during daily peak traffic. Main concern is how throughput guarantees behave when prompt sizes vary and when streaming is enabled.
- Redwood explained how Dedicated throughput SLOs are defined around sustained output tokens/sec over a measurement window, and why mixed workloads need explicit assumptions (context-length distribution, output length caps, concurrency).
- Discussed hardware options: L4 for cost, A100 for balanced, H100 for premium headroom; also single-node vs multi-node and constraints around networking/NVLink and supply by region.
- Agreed to run a benchmark using Northpeak’s representative prompt distribution and a couple of candidate shapes to validate a tier recommendation and draft a proposal.

Topics
1) Northpeak workload + peak patterns
2) What Redwood means by “throughput guarantee” (tokens/sec vs req/sec)
3) Prompt-length variance, streaming, and decode/prefill behavior
4) Dedicated shapes and regional availability
5) Burst behavior, admission control, and “what happens when you exceed”
6) Benchmark plan + proposal timeline

Action Items
- Redwood (Sofia/Omar): Send benchmark questionnaire (prompt histogram, target output length, streaming on/off, concurrency, p95 latency target).
- Northpeak (Arjun/Priya): Share synthetic workload profile + constraints (region, max prompt/output sizes, QPS/concurrency peaks).
- Redwood (Jordan): Send initial shape/tier recommendation + pricing ballpark after initial baselines.

Transcript

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Cool. Um, thanks everyone for making time. Today we wanted to go deeper than the overview—specifically Dedicated, throughput guarantees, and what shapes we’d recommend given your traffic profile. And then end with like, concrete next steps: you send us a little workload profile, we run a couple benchmarks, and we come back with a proposal.

[00:19] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[00:20] Arjun Rao: Yep.

[00:21] Jordan Blake: Great. Quick intros, and then I’ll hand to Sofia and Omar. I’m Jordan, I work with Northpeak on the commercial side.

[00:29] Sofia Ivanova: Hi, I’m Sofia. I lead scheduling and… uh, the runtime behavior that affects throughput/latency under load.

[00:37] Omar El-Sayed: Omar here, I own a lot of our throughput measurement and tuning—how we compute effective tokens per second, queueing, that kind of stuff.

[00:45] Priya Nair: I’m Priya, SRE and infrastructure for Northpeak.

[00:48] Eli Kaplan: Eli, product. I’m mostly here to make sure we’re aligned on what “guarantee” means so I can translate it internally.

[00:55] Arjun Rao: Arjun, I run inference platform. We currently have a vLLM cluster, mix of A10s and A100s, but it’s… it’s messy during peak.

[01:04] Jordan Blake: Awesome. Maya, do you want to set context? Like what you’re trying to accomplish and what’s broken today?

[01:11] Maya Chen: Sure. We have an AI assistant feature. Usage has a very predictable daily peak, like 9am to 1pm Pacific. We see queueing and then we see timeouts. The business is like, “buy more GPUs,” but we’ve learned it’s not linear.

[01:27] Maya Chen: The thing we’re looking for from Dedicated is: can we pay for a box, basically, and know what we can push through it. And not have sales tell us one number, and then SRE sees another number.

[01:39] Jordan Blake: Yep, that’s exactly the problem this project is solving on our end too.

[01:43] Arjun Rao: For us the variability is prompts. We have short chat turns and then we have long retrieval augmented prompts. Like 1k tokens and then 12k tokens, and it can be within the same minute. If your guarantee is “tokens per second,” I want to understand how that doesn’t get gamed or like… become meaningless.

[02:02] Sofia Ivanova: Yep. That’s the right question. The short version is: any throughput guarantee has assumptions. If we don’t write them down, we’re all going to be unhappy.

[02:11] Omar El-Sayed: And also, tokens per second can be defined in different ways—input tokens, output tokens, total tokens. We generally focus on output tokens because that correlates with GPU decode utilization and it’s the piece customers feel.

[02:25] Arjun Rao: You said “output tokens” meaning generated tokens.

[02:28] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, generated tokens. Not prompt tokens. Prompt tokens are prefill. Still costs GPU, but it behaves differently.

[02:35] Priya Nair: Prefill is our killer. Like one user sends 30 pages of context, and everyone else suffers.

[02:41] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly. So, we separate the phases in our own telemetry—prefill and decode—because a workload that’s 90% prefill heavy will have different “steady” throughput.

[02:52] Jordan Blake: Maybe we should do: (1) your workload; (2) what we measure; (3) what shape.

[02:57] Maya Chen: Works.

[03:00] Jordan Blake: Arjun, can you describe typical request: context length distribution, output length, and concurrency? Even rough numbers.

[03:08] Arjun Rao: Yeah. It’s chat-completions style. Most turns are like 200 to 800 input tokens. But when RAG kicks in, we can do 6k to 14k input tokens.

[03:23] Arjun Rao: Output: average maybe 300 tokens, but sometimes 1k. We do streaming always, because product wants the cursor moving quickly.

[03:33] Arjun Rao: Concurrency… at peak we might have 350 in-flight across the cluster. But per model replica, I don’t know; it depends on routing and backpressure.

[03:43] Priya Nair: We cap per pod concurrency at 16 right now, because if we go above that, latency blows up and Kubernetes just… thrashes.

[03:52] Sofia Ivanova: Got it.

[03:54] Maya Chen: Model wise, we’re on Llama 3.1 70B-ish. Quantized in some cases. We’ve tried smaller but quality drop.

[04:04] Omar El-Sayed: Okay 70B changes the calculus on L4 vs A100/H100.

[04:09] Jordan Blake: Region requirements? Where do you need the Dedicated capacity?

[04:13] Priya Nair: US-West ideally. But we can do US-East if we have to.

[04:19] Maya Chen: We also have some EU stuff but it’s small. For now, US is the priority.

[04:24] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[04:26] Sofia Ivanova: Let me explain what we mean by throughput guarantee, then we can map it to shapes.

[04:31] Sofia Ivanova: So, in Dedicated, we’re not talking about a shared pool. You have a reserved GPU fleet slice. The “SLO” or guarantee we’re defining is measured over a window—like sustained output tokens per second over, say, 5 minutes. Not per request.

[04:50] Eli Kaplan: So it’s like “over 5 minutes you will generate at least X tokens per second.”

[04:55] Sofia Ivanova: Yes, with assumptions. Specifically: model version pinned, max context length, and a defined prompt length distribution. Otherwise, if you send only 32k context prompts, nobody can promise the same tokens/sec.

[05:10] Arjun Rao: Right. But we don’t control user behavior perfectly.

[05:14] Omar El-Sayed: Totally. That’s where admission control comes in. If your traffic deviates, we’d rather throttle the outliers than let them collapse the whole deployment.

[05:24] Priya Nair: When you say throttle, you mean 429s?

[05:27] Omar El-Sayed: It can be 429, or it can be queued with a max wait and then fail. We usually do “expected throttling” rather than “silent SLO breach.” The guarantee is about what we can sustain for admitted work.

[05:42] Maya Chen: That’s an important point. We’d rather get a fast 429 on oversized prompts than everybody timing out.

[05:49] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly. We call that overload mode. Under overload, we protect tail latency by limiting concurrency and prefill spikes.

[05:58] Arjun Rao: How do you determine overload? GPU utilization? Queue depth?

[06:03] Sofia Ivanova: A combination. Queue depth, time-in-queue, and effective tokens/sec dropping below expected baselines. Also memory pressure (KV cache).

[06:14] Omar El-Sayed: We instrument “effective output tokens/sec” per deployment and we can break it down by model, region, and tier. If it’s below threshold for N minutes and you’re not in maintenance, it’s a signal.

[06:28] Eli Kaplan: Can you just define “tokens/sec” precisely? Like is it p50, p95, average? I’ve seen vendors hand-wave it.

[06:36] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah. So we compute it as: total output tokens successfully streamed or returned over the window divided by window seconds. And we can compute percentiles across time slices.

[06:50] Omar El-Sayed: For SLO we typically use sustained rate over the 5-minute window, and we look at it like “at least X” for most windows in a month. Not “instantaneous.”

[07:01] Priya Nair: Okay, so you’re not promising per-request latency.

[07:04] Jordan Blake: Dedicated also has latency guardrails, but today we’re focusing on throughput because that’s what you said drives your spend.

[07:11] Sofia Ivanova: For latency, the honest thing is: with large contexts, prefill dominates first token latency. But streaming helps because you can start sending once decode begins.

[07:22] Arjun Rao: Actually, we care about time-to-first-token a lot. Like if it’s over 1.5 seconds, product says it “feels slow.”

[07:31] Sofia Ivanova: Understood. With 70B and 12k prompt, 1.5 seconds can be tough depending on shape. H100 helps a lot.

[07:41] Omar El-Sayed: Also batching choices affect that. If you maximize throughput, you might hurt TTFT. If you cap batch to protect TTFT, you might reduce tokens/sec. Dedicated tiers are basically about which tradeoff we optimize for.

[07:57] Maya Chen: That’s the tiering thing Jordan mentioned.

[08:00] Jordan Blake: Yeah. Think Standard vs Performance vs Premium. We can share the draft definitions, but conceptually:
- Standard: cost-efficient sustained throughput with conservative burst
- Performance: higher sustained throughput + tighter tail latency guardrails
- Premium: best-effort headroom, more aggressive burst, and usually top-end shapes like H100

[08:21] Eli Kaplan: Is Premium like “you always get more”? Or it’s just… you get better hardware.

[08:27] Jordan Blake: Better hardware plus different operational policies. But we have to be careful: “unbounded burst” is not real, so we define burst as a ceiling for a short duration and then you get throttled.

[08:39] Priya Nair: How short is short? Like 30 seconds? 5 minutes?

[08:43] Sofia Ivanova: Usually measured in minutes. Like you can exceed baseline for a couple minutes if there’s headroom, but we’ll protect the system by transitioning to steady mode.

[08:56] Arjun Rao: That’s similar to how we do it internally. Okay.

[09:00] Jordan Blake: Let’s talk shapes. You mentioned A100. What do you run now?

[09:05] Arjun Rao: A100 80GB, some A10s. We tried L4 in another environment but 70B basically didn’t fit nicely unless we really quantized, and then quality got weird.

[09:17] Omar El-Sayed: Yep. L4 is great for smaller models or embeddings/rerank. For 70B with long contexts, you’re either doing multi-GPU or heavy quant.

[09:28] Sofia Ivanova: For Dedicated, typical shapes for 70B are:
- 4x A100 80GB (depending on quant and context)
- 8x A100 80GB if you want more concurrency headroom
- 8x H100 for the “don’t surprise me at peak” tier

[09:44] Priya Nair: Multi-node? Or single node with NVLink?

[09:47] Sofia Ivanova: Prefer single-node with NVLink where possible. Multi-node introduces network variability and can hurt tail latency unless you’re careful.

[09:56] Arjun Rao: But do you even have H100 in US-West? That’s been a problem.

[10:01] Jordan Blake: Great question. Supply is tighter in US-West. US-East is easier for H100. For US-West we can usually do A100 reliably; H100 depends on timing.

[10:12] Maya Chen: If we can do US-East and still meet latency, that might be acceptable. Most users are US.

[10:19] Eli Kaplan: But product will ask me “what’s the guarantee.”

[10:23] Jordan Blake: We should write it as: “For admitted requests matching the agreed workload profile, your deployment will sustain at least X output tokens/sec over a 5-minute window.” And then we list assumptions: model, max context, prompt distribution, streaming on.

[10:42] Arjun Rao: Okay but, if someone sends a 20k prompt, are you dropping it?

[10:47] Omar El-Sayed: If it violates the max context policy, we reject with a clear error. If it’s within context but way outside the distribution, we can either queue it separately, or rate-limit it. We’re building policies so you can choose.

[11:02] Priya Nair: We’d want it to fail fast, not queue forever.

[11:06] Sofia Ivanova: That’s the default.

[11:08] Arjun Rao: Let’s go deeper on the distribution thing. How do we specify it? I don’t want to send you private prompts.

[11:15] Jordan Blake: You don’t have to. You can send a histogram: buckets of input tokens and output tokens, and concurrency over time.

[11:23] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, like: 50% of requests are 0–1k prompt, 40% are 1–4k, 10% are 4–16k. That’s enough for us to run a synthetic benchmark.

[11:36] Arjun Rao: And the guarantee is only valid for that distribution.

[11:40] Omar El-Sayed: Correct.

[11:41] Maya Chen: That seems reasonable.

[11:44] Eli Kaplan: How do we monitor it? Like do we get a dashboard?

[11:48] Jordan Blake: Yes, in Console you’d see throughput vs guarantee, throttling rate, queue depth. And you can export metrics.

[11:56] Priya Nair: We need customer-visible metrics. Like we need to be able to prove it was you or us.

[12:01] Sofia Ivanova: Totally. We include carve-outs: maintenance windows, customer-induced errors, and when you exceed agreed limits.

[12:12] Arjun Rao: How do you handle streaming in the measurement? Because streaming returns tokens over time. If a request is long, it spans multiple windows.

[12:22] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, streaming complicates it. We count tokens when they’re emitted. So a long stream contributes across windows. That’s actually the right representation of load.

[12:33] Arjun Rao: But then TTFT doesn’t show up.

[12:35] Omar El-Sayed: TTFT is separate metric. Throughput SLO is not TTFT. But tier selection can enforce TTFT guardrails by limiting batch sizes.

[12:49] Sofia Ivanova: In practice, for 70B, you’ll choose: do you want maximum throughput (bigger batches, more queueing) or more interactive feel (smaller batches, more reserved headroom).

[13:02] Maya Chen: We probably want interactive for the assistant.

[13:06] Priya Nair: But we can tolerate some queueing during peak, as long as it’s controlled.

[13:12] Jordan Blake: That usually maps to Performance tier on A100 or Premium on H100.

[13:19] Arjun Rao: What about splitting workloads? Like long-context requests go to one pool, short ones to another.

[13:25] Sofia Ivanova: That’s a good pattern. We can do two deployments, different shapes or policies, and route by context length.

[13:34] Arjun Rao: That would make my life easier.

[13:37] Maya Chen: It might make budgeting harder.

[13:40] Jordan Blake: We can propose both options. Sometimes it’s cheaper overall because you keep the expensive hardware reserved for the interactive path.

[13:49] Eli Kaplan: Can you do that within one Dedicated contract? Like two “pools”?

[13:54] Jordan Blake: Yes, you can have multiple Dedicated deployments under the same account, with separate capacity commitments.

[14:02] Priya Nair: Okay.

[14:04] Arjun Rao: Let’s talk numbers. What tokens per second are we talking for A100 vs H100 for 70B?

[14:10] Jordan Blake: We can’t give a single number without your profile.

[14:12] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, because 1k vs 12k prompt changes it a lot. But directionally, H100 can be… depending on config, 1.5x to 2x throughput for decode and better TTFT for long prompts.

[14:28] Arjun Rao: That’s consistent with what we’ve seen.

[14:31] Sofia Ivanova: Also KV cache. Long contexts eat memory. With H100 80GB you get more room for concurrency before you hit eviction or you have to reduce batch.

[14:41] Priya Nair: Eviction kills us. We see huge jitter.

[14:45] Sofia Ivanova: Right.

[14:47] Eli Kaplan: So the “guarantee” is basically: with these assumptions, your box can do this sustained output rate.

[14:54] Jordan Blake: Correct.

[14:56] Eli Kaplan: If we exceed it, we get throttled, not silently degraded.

[15:00] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. We want predictable behavior: either you’re meeting the SLO for admitted load, or we’re shedding gracefully.

[15:10] Arjun Rao: But if your system throttles us, we might still say “you didn’t meet throughput.”

[15:15] Jordan Blake: That’s why we separate “expected throttling” vs “SLO breach.” If you’re being throttled because you’re exceeding contract profile, that’s not us failing. If you’re within profile and we still can’t deliver, that’s a breach.

[15:33] Priya Nair: That’s actually what we need. Because today everything just turns into a gray area.

[15:38] Maya Chen: Agree.

[15:40] Sofia Ivanova: We can also give you recommended client-side behavior: retry with jitter, cap max tokens, set a hard ceiling for prompt size. Those help a lot.

[15:51] Arjun Rao: We can do that.

[15:54] Jordan Blake: I want to be respectful of time. Can we align on a benchmark plan? That’s usually the fastest path.

[16:00] Maya Chen: Yes.

[16:01] Jordan Blake: Omar/Sofia, what do you need from them?

[16:05] Omar El-Sayed: Three things:
1) Prompt length distribution (histogram) and output length targets
2) Concurrency target and whether you want strict TTFT
3) Whether you’re doing function calling / tools because that changes stop/start patterns

[16:22] Arjun Rao: We do tool calling, yeah. Like maybe 20% of requests call tools once or twice.

[16:29] Sofia Ivanova: Okay. That adds extra turns. We can approximate it.

[16:33] Priya Nair: We can give you a trace sample with lengths, not content.

[16:37] Omar El-Sayed: Perfect.

[16:39] Jordan Blake: Region preference US-West, but open to US-East. And model: Llama 3.1 70B, probably.

[16:48] Maya Chen: Yes.

[16:49] Arjun Rao: We might consider a 8B for some flows but the big one is 70B.

[16:54] Jordan Blake: Great.

[16:56] Eli Kaplan: Can you also send something I can share internally explaining why tokens/sec depends on prompt distribution? Like a simple paragraph.

[17:03] Jordan Blake: Yes. We’ll send a write-up.

[17:06] Sofia Ivanova: Also, one more: maximum context length you plan to allow. 8k? 16k?

[17:12] Arjun Rao: We allow up to 16k today.

[17:15] Priya Nair: But most are under 8k.

[17:18] Sofia Ivanova: Great. We can set policy: max 16k, but we tune for your distribution.

[17:26] Arjun Rao: Sounds good.

[17:28] Jordan Blake: Okay. Then on our side, we’ll run on two shapes. My proposal: A100 baseline and H100 baseline. If cost is a concern, we can add L4 for a smaller model but not for 70B.

[17:44] Maya Chen: Let’s do A100 and H100.

[17:46] Priya Nair: Yes.

[17:47] Arjun Rao: Fine.

[17:49] Jordan Blake: Timeline wise: if you send inputs early next week, we can probably get results by end of next week.

[17:56] Maya Chen: Works.

[17:58] Jordan Blake: Any remaining concerns we should address now?

[18:02] Priya Nair: Just one: how do you handle maintenance. Like if you’re patching, do we lose our guarantee.

[18:08] Jordan Blake: Dedicated has maintenance windows communicated in advance. During that, SLO accounting excludes those periods. And we can do rolling where possible.

[18:18] Sofia Ivanova: For a single-node deployment, sometimes you need a restart, but we try to minimize.

[18:23] Priya Nair: Okay.

[18:25] Arjun Rao: Another: multi-tenancy. Dedicated is isolated, right?

[18:29] Jordan Blake: Yes, Dedicated is dedicated capacity. No other customer shares those GPUs.

[18:34] Arjun Rao: Good.

[18:35] Eli Kaplan: And we can get audit logs?

[18:38] Jordan Blake: Yes, we have audit logs and export, but we can cover that in a separate security review if you want.

[18:44] Maya Chen: We’ll probably need it, but later.

[18:47] Jordan Blake: Great.

[18:49] Sofia Ivanova: One more note on prompt variance: if you have a small fraction of extremely long prompts, it’s often best to route them to a separate queue or separate deployment. We can implement that via routing rules.

[19:02] Arjun Rao: Yeah. We can likely do “if prompt > 8k route to long-context pool.”

[19:07] Sofia Ivanova: Exactly.

[19:09] Jordan Blake: Okay, let’s recap next steps so we’re aligned.

[19:13] Jordan Blake: We’ll send a benchmark questionnaire and a simple explanation of throughput measurement by tomorrow EOD. You’ll send back histogram + concurrency targets by Feb 18. We’ll run A100 and H100 baselines, and share results and a tier recommendation by Feb 21. Then we’ll draft a proposal for the week of Feb 24.

[19:35] Maya Chen: Great.

[19:36] Arjun Rao: Works.

[19:37] Priya Nair: Yep.

[19:39] Eli Kaplan: Thanks. Please include the “what happens when we exceed” part. That’s the most important for product.

[19:45] Jordan Blake: Will do.

[19:47] Sofia Ivanova: And if you can, include whether you want hard caps on max output tokens, because runaway outputs can also nuke throughput.

[19:55] Arjun Rao: Oh yeah, we cap at 1,024 today.

[19:58] Omar El-Sayed: Perfect.

[20:00] Jordan Blake: Awesome. Thanks everyone.

(Recording ends abruptly; crosstalk)

[20:06] Speaker 2: —cool, talk soon.

[20:07] Speaker 1: Thanks.

Note: Fireflies transcript may contain errors and missing words, especially around technical terms (KV cache, prefill/decode, GPU shapes).
